title: Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts (bleepingcomputer.com)
comments: No matter whether you like or hate or don't care about cryptocurrencies, this is incredible stuff...Now basically: every single attack that's been described as "theoretical" or "far-fetched" or "only existing in the mind of a paranoid person" did actually happen.We're talking here about a tiny eSIM implant and a little CPU doing OCR on the fonts appearing on the hardware wallet's screen to read the secrets during set up. So the secure element ain't tampered with.Not long ago the Coldcard hardware wallet had an issue where it'd fallback to a 32-bit only RNG that could be cracked and so many people got their coins stolen.Now it's Ledger that sees tampered devices all around the world (in Asia for sure but now there are reports about reseller in the EU selling backdoored/eSIM'ed devices).For people who own Bitcoin at this point one of the only thing kinda sensible to do is to use multisig schemes, like 2-of-2 or 3-of-3 multisig, where your split the secret over two or three different hardware wallet brands (meaning being able to sign a 2-of-2 wallets requires hardware wallets from two different vendors).When Ledger hardware wallets came out and people said that seed (the list of words) could be intercepted and relayed by a channel bypassing the computer (here by using an eSIM), people would post explaining that people were nuts if they thought such an attack could be pulled off.Yet here we are.And Ledger is responsible for very poor security practices: for example it's impossible to use a Ledger hardware wallet in a fully airgapped/offline way. For you're forced to not only upgrade the firmware but also install the Bitcoin "ledger app" (or whatever that is called) after you entered your seed into the device.Which is complete and total amateur hour.In addition to that Ledger offers a service to "backup your seed": what could possibly go wrong with that uh?I'm betting that we'll soon hear about hardware wallets getting drained due to the seed being exfiltrated through "randomness" in how transactions are built/signed (aka "kleptography").And it's not just representative about people in the cryptocurrencies ecosystem: people simply don't understand computer security and don't understand the potential attacks nor the length at which attackers are willing to go to steal data/funds/ruin other people's lives.At this point we've heard about chips' plans being modified before the chips are even built (only to lower the entropy of RNGs) [unrelated to cryptocurrencies btw], a worldwide backdoor attempt in SSH, eSIM sending secrets from hardware wallets with tiny attack surfaces.You're not anywhere near paranoid enough.reply

A currency can arise from any fungible, tradable, generally-durable commodity that the bulk of society decides to accept as being worthwhile.  In prisons cigarettes often fill that role; in pre-agrarian hunter gatherer groups it's often little baubles like shells.  Government isn't necessary for this, but social contract is.  You need to have enough faith that your neighbor will accept the currency to accept it yourself.Cryptocurrencies have the advantage that they can be spent worldwide, instantaneously, with little friction, while most commodities require that you be physically present to exchange them.  They're also significantly easier to store and more resistant to garden-variety theft, as long as they're secured by passphrases.  But they exist in the uncanny valley of requiring electricity and Internet.  It is fairly unlikely that the government collapses and yet you still retain always-on electricity and Internet.  What will you use to pay the electric company, and how do you enforce the contract that they keep providing you power?There's perhaps an interesting role for a digital cryptocurrency that does not require always-on connectivity, eg. something that can be carried over SneakerNet for local transactions, and then automatically syncs up with the global system when the community regains Internet connectivity.  In actual conflict zones today, people seem to get intermittent electrical & Internet connectivity, eg. the electricity will come on for an hour a day with rolling blackouts, and then you try to get everything charged in that one hour.  And there are enough solar installations out there that several communities are likely to retain significant power even in the event of a societal collapse.  But current crypto's consensus mechanisms aren't built for intermittent connectivity: you'd need to build and design something that is eventually consistent, where a weeks-long fork does not result in two competing cryptocurrencies.reply

I am sorry to burst your "bubble", as it were, but cryptocurrencies are not, in fact, currencies.Speaking in terms of U.S. regulation and legislation, crypto is variously regulated as a "commodity" or as a "security" and therefore, cannot be formally considered a currency. The name, "cryptocurrency" is a marketing ploy, which cleverly seeks to dilute the meaning of the term, which is a term of art, and is still reserved, in legal circles, for things which are, in fact, currencies, and function as currencies, and are regulated as currencies, which crypto... is not.It was rather painful to me in particular, because a few weeks ago, I registered and attended a municipal education session on fraud. And this session was co-hosted by an actual representative of the Arizona Corporation Commission - Securities Division. I can prove that because my prize for the session was an authentic, imprinted, ACC/SD pizza slicer! Anyway, as soon as she mentioned crypto and asserted it is a class of "currency" I tried to call her out, and I asked more than once, and being reluctant to turn the session into a referendum on her legal knowledge, I finally let her win. It was embarrassing.Anyway, no, cryptocurrency has never been a currency. Not in the USA. Other nations may deem it as such, but I kind of doubt it so far. Please do not conflate real currency with crypto. They are distinct things that are easily distinguished. The consumer should not be deluded into thinking otherwise.reply

Currency is used for trade between multiple distrusting groups, credit is used for trade within a social group.  There was an article recently on HN about the highland tribes of Papua New Guinea [1] and it described how the natives would trade amongst tribes using shells.You actually see this on a small scale today in the functioning of many small communities, eg. you don't actually exchange currency to pay the host of a party, but you are expected to reciprocate and host sometimes yourself if you want to keep getting invited.  There's a surprisingly large amount of these unpaid micro-transactions that happen, eg. my wife has gotten free childcare, free advice, free (used) furniture, free baby clothes, etc, all in the heart of Silicon Valley, because she reciprocates and also gives away her old furniture, baby toys, baby clothes, advice, introductions, childcare, etc.  But when we have to pay the contractor for work on our house, we need dollars.  When we buy a computer, we need dollars.  When we buy all those goods that we give away new, we need dollars.  That again reinforces the "credit is for people you know, currency is for people you don't" distinction.Barter is used when a previous currency system collapses.  The currency is no longer guaranteed to be accepted, so people want hard goods that they know they can use.  But barter is an unstable equilibrium: as you mentioned, currency is just barter where one particular good becomes so widely accepted that people will take it not because they want it, but because it can be traded for other things that they want.  There are reports of the Bosnian War [2] that described how alcohol and ammo quickly became pseudo-currencies because they were universally accepted and could easily be traded for what you actually needed.Graeber isn't wrong, but as an anthropologist he over-indexes on the within-group interactions.  There are lots of documented examples of currency emerging spontaneously from trade between groups where the groups all mutually decided that one type of object had value.[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49708431[2] https://www.scribd.com/document/664716931/How-I-survived-a-y...reply

comments: Excuse me for throwing up this stupid idea, but if code changes per unit of time keep growing at this rate and are not slowing down with infinite merging demand, it seems that this repo will be in a constant state of continuous change and we constantly roll forward with automated code and obviously no direct human supervision, then why even have source control? Agents use source control, too. It's a pretty important part of the development process to understand how code has changed.For example, you can imagine, at the extreme, that agents could get caught in code change loops: a code change seems appropriate, it is implemented, it turns out there's some external factor which makes it not appropriate, the change is reverted, then that same code change seems appropriate again, etc.Obviously you can prevent that from occurring with some extra infrastructure in-place, but at that point you're basically creating source control.reply

>Obviously you can prevent that from occurring with some extra infrastructure in-place, but at that point you're basically creating source control.most of the harnesses are checkpointing most of the data of a git commit aside from the formal release and messaging, anyway; thats why they all have a similar problem with SQL dbs exploding in size after a bit of time.Right now we're in this weird transition where most of the harness systems are layering git tool use w/ the constant snapshotting AND a memory subsystem often, probably leaves a lot on the table in saving wasted token use to just ditch the vcs all together and rely on the already persistent and existent checkpoints and memories for reconstruction.reply

title: Recreational Programming (cphiri.dev)
comments: The definition perfectly describes how I started out in computers in 1981. Brought home a 4K, 8-bit computer from Radio Shack that I could barely afford and hooked it to the TV. Had never touched a computer before, zero prior knowledge and only had the manual in the box (which was surprisingly good). No one I'd ever met owned a computer at home or used one at work and I'd never really considered that you could make money with computers. I just thought the games seemed fun and the idea of learning about programming seemed cool. Turns out typing in long listings from B&W hobbyist zines and then finding all the typos was a fine way to learn.Teaching myself assembler was harder because I had no docs. I was so clueless I actually looked up Motorola in the phone book and called to ask where I could get a manual. The sales rep who answered the phone must have taken pity on me because he mailed the CPU manual for free. I still have the purple reference card and remember the common opcodes by heart (https://colorcomputerarchive.com/repo/Documents/Datasheets/M...)The first time I made money was about 18 months later when I wrote a pretty handy disk utility program. Stayed up all Friday night finishing it. Copied onto floppies I sold for $5 at the local user's group Saturday morning. Made $140 and got my first 28 customers. That was enough to get me hooked on making software and selling it. ~40 years, three startups, over a dozen products, hundreds of good people employed, a couple million customers and two PC Magazine Product of the Year awards later - I regret nothing. Started on a lark to learn and have fun. Much was learned, fun was had. Wonderful journey - highly recommend.reply

> but no PC Magazine Product of the Year!Well, hitting the first home run took about a decade full of base hits and more than a few strike-outs on the way to figuring out what I needed to know to do a tech startup well.> What is the "weird" kid doing today?Over the last decade I've spent increasing pro bono time trying to 'pay it forward' talking to classes and groups of erstwhile entrepreneurs, so I've heard versions of that question a LOT. It actually took me a couple years before I realized there is no 'right' answer because the right thing for each person differs depending their unique personality, skills, interests, context and life journey.The most helpful thing I can share isn't a guess about which target you should aim for but rather some advice about how to approach your journey. First, I hope you want to be a tech entrepreneur because that's the only thing I know about. I have no idea what skills will be in demand to get a high-paying, secure job or how to get promoted. I had to become an entrepreneur because I was terrible at being an employee.I never aimed for my guess at what would be "hot" next and I doubt my guess would be right anyway. Every time I found success it was by starting with a real problem some customer actually had. Initially that customer was me or a friend but it doesn't matter. It just has to be a serious enough problem that motivated customers are actively looking for new and better solutions than what exists. Then figure out a way to solve their problem better enough that they'll actually buy it. It doesn't have to be perfect in every way, just better enough in most ways and perfect in at least one way.In fact, some of my best products became hits by cleverly solving one part of a problem SUPER well, at the cost of some serious downsides in other areas. For example, my friends and I all desperately wanted a Zig-Zag Widget but good ones were stupid expensive and the ones ordinary schmoes like us could afford Zigged and Zagged like shit. But we figured out I how to make a Zig-Only Widget we could actually afford. No Zag but it Zigged better than the best and that was a trade-off I was okay with. Turns out other people were too... especially after we worked on adding some 'pseudo-Zag' features that worked around the worst parts of not Zagging. The world's best Zig (but no Zag) at 1/4th the price of even a half-assed Zig-Zag. Not really new technology, just a very clever mixture of the exact right old tech with a little new stuff, some clever UX innovations and cool workflow integrations. First Product of the Year.If prototyping dozens of different iterations and trying each one out with real, live problem-having customers and listening empathetically to their constant complaints, ridiculous demands and occasional awesome suggestions sounds like fun, then you may have found your calling. If you just want to write great code for a good paycheck and be left in peace, then, my friend, don't just walk... run the other way. :-) It's ironic because I got into making products because I loved programming but after the first few years, I wasn't writing much code anymore. It was invaluable that I'd learned the business by starting as a self-taught, down-to-the-metal, assembly language, real-time graphics programmer because I was able to identify and hire programmers far more skilled than I'd ever been but after the first million in revenue and 20th employee I personally spent more time writing or reviewing ad copy and legal contracts than code. But that's also invaluable because as the company grew and various fires flared up in every part of our business, I got pretty damn good at doing marketing, sales, PR, finance and even legal stuff myself when necessary. And all that was the best prep ever for being able to run the place when we hit a hundred million in sales and hundreds of employees.Now that I recently retired I'm back to writing 8-bit assembler code, except now I have working collection with every 80s Atari, Commodore, Sinclair and Amstrad model ever made.reply

Just FYI on MacOS's default telemetry:1) By default, every word (each character, actually) you input into Spotlight/Siri gets time-stamped and sent to `smoot.apple.com`2) Even with a Pi-Hole blocking *.apple.com (i.e. using MacOS >> Networking >> DNS Server), on boot all modern Apple Silicon reaches out to security.apple.com (i.e. bypassing the user's manual-input DNS setting), using the DHCP-issued DNS IP [0]pro-tip: use your router's DHCP to auto-issue your local Pi-Hole's IP address [as DNS] with your IP-leases; then you'll actually be able to block all *.apple.com traffic (using the PiHole which your DHCP issues to, by default)[0] this is for security chip "lockout" detection (e.g.) and it is pervasive across NICs (i.e. it REALLY seeks any attempt for DNS resolution to security.apple.com)reply

title: MIT class project turns into an FDA-cleared treatment for tremors (news.mit.edu)
comments:
Having built a pulsed vibration wristband for someone with Parkinson's, just a few notes.  For Parkinson's patients:  - there's a small-ish window in the disease progression where pulsed vibration is able to help a person regain some intentional motor control
  - the device doesn't stop the tremors
  - the pulsed vibration does let the brain's control signal come through stronger, so drawing/typing/moving the mouse is more intentional.  
  - this is no more effective than the results of levidopa/carbidopa treatment, and the levidopa/carbidopa typically calms the overall tremors
  - as Parkinson's progresses, these devices become useless, and if the patient qualifies for deep brain stimulation, it's worth looking into (regain years of useful life if you're lucky).

I haven't tested the device on people with essential tremor, so I don't have anything smart to say there.You can make a very unsophisticated version of this without a lot of hardware:  - small microcontroller with 3v outputs (XIAO's are perfect)
  - 3v sealed eccentric mass motors (aliexpress $1/ea)
  - elastic wristband
  - usb battery
  - software to pulse the motors for about 200 miliseconds for an on off sequence of about 8 times, then rest for about a second and repeat.

Hopefully these folks will price it affordably.Side note: the idea was published in 2016-2017 in a few promotional videos from Microsoft research: https://www.windowscentral.com/microsofts-emma-watch-and-pro...reply
